en: The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-arthavyākhyāna* states that one is thus able to engage with all things. To abandon these is the wisdom of emptiness; "or" (*si*) refers to their removal. Regarding the phrase "for this reason":
it is because these serve as the remedies for the four types of afflictions that they are called the "four immeasurables. "Not one" means they are not identical.
The fifth [category] corresponds entirely to the second [category].
That which is not the second is not the fourth.
The third corresponds to the third; the third [category] corresponds entirely to the first.
From "As you have said" below,
the third section first answers the initial objection.
Regarding the two kinds of anger:
The first is superior and the second is middling.
The suffering of taking life is coarse yet heavy;
the suffering of flogging is light yet subtle.
Cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cuts off those who take life;
the mind of loving-kindness is subtle, while the impulse to take life is coarse.
Cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) cuts off those who inflict flogging.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the superior capacity for severing even subtle traces of doubt;
thus, it is by means of lower wisdom that one severs higher afflictions (*kleśa*).
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*), however, is the lowest of the low wisdoms.
To sever the supreme delusion of taking life is the supreme wisdom;
to sever the lowest-of-the-low delusion of flogging and beating is [the corresponding practice].
There are five below.
Furthermore, to explain in detail:
one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to sever the [afflictions] above.
Cultivating compassion is the severance of the middle.
As for the companions, they answer the second point regarding what should be done in response to a single objection.
There are four ways in which companions relate to one another.
Among kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, the three middle practices complete their cultivation through equanimity (*upekṣā*);
since equanimity fundamentally guides and completes the preceding ones, these three are called "companions" in the sense that they mutually support and guide one another.
When analyzed, they constitute four.
Your first objection—that it is not one but four—is refuted.
Furthermore, by means of the analogy of a vessel, the third objection is answered:
impoverished sentient beings are the vessels for the house of a compassionate heart.
Sentient beings in great suffering are vessels for the family of compassion.
Sentient beings who are jealous are vessels for the family of sympathetic joy.
Those who cling to signs are vessels for the family of equanimity.
When the Great Being brings joy to others,
he is devoid of the latter three modes of conduct;
when he uproots the suffering of others, [he is likewise devoid of them].
There is neither the former one nor the latter two.
When rejoicing with a heart of joy for those before one,
there are likewise neither the former two.
When the mind of equanimity is devoid of signs,
it no longer possesses the preceding three;
for this reason, there should properly be four.
Your previous objection does not apply to the three types of compassion;
rather, the following response to the fourth objection distinguishes them by way of practice.
Those who follow the path of vision (darśana-mārga) frequently give rise to great anger.
Hatred has superior and intermediate degrees;
loving-kindness (*maitrī*) eliminates the superior, while compassion (*karuṇā*) eliminates the intermediate.
For those who practice [the meditations on] sensation, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) frequently arises, which likewise has superior and intermediate degrees.
Because joy abandons [the lower] and equanimity abandons [the middle],
they are distinguished by their modes of activity; thus, there are four.
"How can you say that there should be two and not four?
As for the claim that they may also be called 'four' because they are immeasurable," this is the fifth response,
which addresses the objection regarding the sound.
Within loving-kindness (*maitrī*), immeasurable and boundless minds bestow happiness;
within compassion (*karuṇā*), immeasurable and boundless minds extract suffering;
within sympathetic joy (*muditā*), immeasurable and boundless minds rejoice in all things.
In the mind of equanimity, there is no measure; in the immeasurable mind, the marks of measurement perish.
Because it is immeasurable, it is given the name "the fourth."
It is not the case that there is only one "should not be" rather than four, as you have objected above.
Since the "immeasurable" consists of four types, how can you claim otherwise?
Thus concludes the extensive response to the objections raised above.
It is clearly known that there are four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Below, one intends to examine how ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) obtain the designation "immeasurable," as well as those of the nature of the immeasurable and the immeasurable seeds (*anantānantabīja-gotra*).
Although there are immeasurable [attainments], they are not ultimate.

Regarding the third stage, when those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) truly attain [the realization of] the "point of a fingernail" (nakhāgra), it is called "immeasurable"; whereas the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain the "immeasurable of the immeasurable."
Is there a bodhisattva who attains compassion that is not inferior?
Second, the sequence of the arising of the textual passages clarifies the method for cultivating the causes.
This is because the four types mentioned in the preceding section have all been brought forth here.

In the "Brief Analysis" (Liaojian) section below, it merely states that those of the Two Vehicles are called "Staggers" (gui), while Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "Immeasurable" (wuliang). It does not further explain the "Immeasurable" nature of those at the stage of the Seed of Practice (xi zhongxing).
At that time, people harbored doubts in their minds.
This means that when the first ten stages of mind, which are immeasurably immeasurable for both the person and the Buddha,
are about to be cleared away by the Buddha,

he therefore first asks about the two intentions: how the stage of the nature of understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and the Buddha attain the immeasurably immeasurable, and why the person of the stage of the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja-bhūmi*) does not attain the immeasurably immeasurable.
He first poses the question in order to cause the Tathāgata to explain the reason for this.

Regarding sentient beings, he distinguishes three categories: those inferior to oneself, those equal to oneself, and those superior to oneself—namely, one's own relatives, neutral persons, and enemies.
Within those who are dear, one further distinguishes three grades;
among those who are neutral, one likewise distinguishes three grades;
and among those who are hostile, one also distinguishes three grades.
The three [types of] threefold [beings] comprise nine grades.
First, regarding the practice of the mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings: one bestows superior happiness equally upon those who are neutral and those who are kin.
Toward a supreme enemy—one who has killed one's parents—one, though a supreme enemy and a source of great opposition to oneself, bestows even a minor grade of happiness.
Regarding middling enemies, such as those who kill one's brothers and so forth, these are the circumstances of middling enemies; they can only provide a small amount of middling-grade pleasure.
As for inferior enemies, being even more subtle, they instead provide superior-grade pleasure.
Furthermore, as for those who practice again:

some may traverse kalpas practicing the path, cultivating a mind of loving-kindness toward former enemies who previously acted with hostility toward them; even in such cases, they correctly attain superior, middling, or lower grades of happiness.
Regarding the place reached by neutral enemies, one cultivates a slight mind of loving-kindness; for others who are superior, one transforms them by bestowing increased and supreme happiness.

One may also practice this cultivation for one or two kalpas, so that through the cause of the thickening mind of loving-kindness, one comes to feel the same toward superior enemies and bestows supreme happiness upon them.
Even if one attains the nine grades of attainment equally at the upper level of the third banner, one still cannot be called "Greatly Compassionate.
A Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage (bhūmi) should dwell in the foundational stage and ultimately eliminate all signs (nimitta).
This Great Compassion is the most profound among the icchantikas and the most extreme evil.
From the very beginning, the bodhisattva does not perceive any faults in the icchantika and regards them as a supreme field of merit;
for this reason, it is called "Great Compassion."

To exclude that which is unbeneficial—unbeneficialness being suffering—to exclude such unbeneficial suffering should be called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā). As for why it is called "loving-kindness" (maitrī): [it is because it excludes that which is unbeneficial].
To uproot suffering and exhaust its origin while manifesting the principle of bestowing happiness upon oneself is fully designated as "Great Loving-kindness" (mahāmaitrī).
To bestow immeasurable benefit and happiness upon sentient beings is called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā).
Bestowing happiness should properly be named "Loving-kindness."
The reason it is called "compassion" (karuṇā) is that only when sentient beings attain immeasurable happiness does my meaning of "extracting them from suffering" become manifest;
this is what is first termed "great compassion" (mahā-karuṇā).
To feel great joy upon seeing others obtain happiness is called "great joy" (muditā).
To practice equanimity toward both enemies and kin is called "equanimity" (upekṣā).
It is to perceive all things as equal, without regard for one's own self.
That which is called "great equanimity" is this equanimity of emptiness;
it is the relinquishing of one's own happiness to bestow it upon sentient beings.
This is equanimity within the realm of existence (*bhava*).
It pertains only to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and below.

While the preceding sections have appropriately clarified compassion (*karuṇā*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and so forth, they have not yet clarified the actual generation of the myriad practices (*sādhana*).
From here on below, the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) are clarified;
these are the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) that arise from reality.
First, one attains the mundane four immeasurables.
Within this lineage of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*),

there are immeasurable [beings] who subsequently give rise to bodhicitta; these are those of the lineage of nature (*prakṛtisthagotra*) and those in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*).
This is the awakening of the resolve for enlightenment.
Only then does one emerge from the world;
that is, when the understanding of the mind becomes fully perfected and the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) arises, it is called "transcending the world."
Regarding "the immeasurables based on the mundane":
because the four immeasurables arising from within the stage of the lineage of practice give rise to supramundane immeasurables; for this reason.
Because these causes accumulate over a long period in the world, they are called "greatly immeasurable.
From Kāśyapa’s address to the Buddha, "excluding that which is unbeneficial," and so forth,
this is the third proof of compassion.
In truth, it is because the removal of what is unbeneficial by those above is called "Great Loving-kindness" (mahāmaitrī),
while the bestowing of immeasurable happiness is called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā).
For this reason, the question is posed.
If compassion is truly that which gives rise to the myriad practices and serves as the foundation for all virtues, then I challenge the Tathāgata:
is this compassion not false, such that it cannot serve as the foundation for all virtues?
How is this known? Regarding the unreality of compassion:
it is like a bhikṣu who contemplates the robes he wears as being entirely the appearance of skin, though they are not actually skin.
When one contemplates what is eaten by forming the perception that it is insects, although in reality they are not insects, this is a false contemplation; the four immeasurables are likewise so.
Being illusory and false, they cannot provide true benefit.
"Although he presides over the music with the assembly, in reality he does not obtain any pleasure.
Is this not, therefore, false and illusory?
This is the second objection raised by the World-Honored One.

If it were not false and truly conferred happiness, why would all people not receive ultimate bliss through the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? We clearly see that sentient beings undergo manifold sufferings.
One clearly knows that compassion is illusory and not real.
If it were real, one would not obtain happiness;
this is the third rebuttal.
In the past and present, people have not attained happiness because they perceive compassion as something illusory. Yet,
it was by cultivating a single act of benevolence that the Buddha in former times attained birth among the Brahmā gods and reached the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
To say that one "attains" it is, in reality, to not attain it.
If the mere practice of a single act of loving-kindness were to result in the karmic rewards of the human or celestial realms,
how could this truly correspond to the principle that the loving-kindness of today is unreal?
Excellent! The following verses explain that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the reality; this is not yet an answer to the question.

If one does not give rise to anger toward even a single sentient being, but constantly bestows happiness with a mind of loving-kindness, it is called the perfection of loving-kindness (*maitrī-pāramitā*).
The karmic fruit obtained from various kinds of giving does not equal even one-sixteenth part of a single portion of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Therefore, we know that loving-kindness and compassion are truly transcendent of worldly merit.
Now, one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) realizes that this is the ultimate truth; this answers the first question.

As for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), their resolve is limited; because they achieve only the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita*), they cannot encompass other beings, and thus their realization may be considered unreal.

To clarify that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas internally understand their own permanence while externally encompassing the transformations of all classes of beings, they accord with the lowly nature of the mind to realize compassion through benefiting others.
This is truly able to serve as the foundation for all myriad virtues; they perceive the great earth as gold and silver, and the waters of the ocean as clarified butter and cream.
It enables those who came before to certainly and firmly attain its application;
it clearly reveals that compassion is real,
and it severs greed and desire below.
Because one eliminates the four categories [of afflictions],
it is known that loving-kindness and compassion are real.
Furthermore, the four immeasurables are the root of all wholesome dharmas.
Answering the third question:
How could the merit of a compassionate mind consist merely of the retributive fruits of human and celestial realms?
The myriad virtues produced by the four immeasurable minds ultimately result in the fruit of eternal abiding, which necessarily arises through the practice of compassion.
How could this be false?

From here below, the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) are extensively explained as giving rise to the various practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ pāramitāḥ*). To explain the practice of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) in detail:
"For example, there is a person... and so forth. What does this mean? [It means:]... [The passage continues from here.]
The preceding section has clarified how the four immeasurable minds can give rise to the various practices of the six perfections,
among which the practice of giving (*dāna*) has been extensively analyzed.
From this point onward, this text is composed with the intent to clarify the distinctions between what is correct and what is erroneous through mutual comparison.
The "person, for example" refers to a bodhisattva who has newly set out on the path;
"being struck by a poisoned arrow" refers to his person.
Discriminating against fields of merit and begrudgingly failing to give destroys one's practice of *dāna*;
such stinginess and greed further harm the life-force of wisdom.
This is likened to a poisoned arrow.
The "retinue" refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"Desiring to bring about peace and security" means that by contemplating the practice of giving (dāna) and ascending to that level, it is called "peace and security," which eliminates poison.
"Summoning a skilled physician" refers to the presence of a responsive capacity for transformation, which is termed "summoning"; this serves as a general metaphor for the recipient [of the teaching].
When the conditions of wealth, time, and causes are met,
the physician who extracts the arrow is present; thus,
all the requisite conditions have been fulfilled.
Contemplating the practice of giving to eliminate internal stinginess is called "extracting the arrow.
This text previously identified internal stinginess as a poisonous arrow;
thus, from my contemplation, it is this poisonous arrow [that must be removed].
The passage from "From which direction it comes" onwards refers to the beggar named Senaka as the "poisoned arrow.
It should be understood that this is not produced by external poison;
rather, because of the internal poison of stinginess (*mātsarya*), it is called a "poisoned arrow."
"From which direction have you come? Observe what has been sown before you.
From which direction have you come? By whom were you shot? By whom were you sent?
If it was sent by a Buddha or a Bodhisattva,"
The meaning is the same as being shot by a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa.
If it is someone sent by the six heretical teachers, the meaning is the same as being shot by a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.

Regarding "the bamboo and the willow": observing those who uphold or violate the precepts, the nature of the bamboo is firm and solid, serving as a metaphor for one who upholds the precepts with steadfastness;
the nature of the willow is supple and weak, serving as a metaphor for one who violates the precepts.
Internally, there is no trace of pure restraint; the mind indulges in the six sense objects, extensively giving rise to perverse inclinations—this is what is called "willow.
As for the iron cauldron, one observes whether the person before one possesses generosity or lacks it.
As for what it is that is treated:
the scriptural teachings serve as the treatment.
If one’s wisdom and understanding arise from the Buddha’s scriptures, they will certainly be able to destroy [afflictions], just as steel is capable of cutting.
If one derives false wisdom from the four Vedas of the non-Buddhists, it causes false views to increase; this is called "pliancy.

When practicing non-contemplation—whether in a state of meditative concentration or not—the general principle is that upon observing a beggar before them, one internally upholds the Tripitaka and immediately desires to practice giving.
If one does not possess the Three Pitakas, one does not practice giving based on their teachings.

Regarding those with feathers and fur, one observes the conduct and decorum of their followers; if they appear pleasing to the eye, one desires to give clothing, but if they do not appear pleasing, one does not give.
Regarding giving:
all that is poisonous consists of the signs of fetters and the deportment arising from conditioned activity;

"clarity" refers to having right view, which is precisely the aforementioned possession of supreme precepts and supreme wisdom occurring spontaneously. That which is false view is precisely the aforementioned absence of supreme precepts and supreme wisdom.
Regarding the measurement of one chi and six cun:
the body has four marks, each being four cun; four times four makes sixteen, hence "one chi and six cun.
For all śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas, compassion is the root of the myriad virtues cultivated during the causal stage.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the root of the myriad virtues within the fruits attained by the Tathāgata and those below him;
thus, one knows that loving-kindness is the reality. Since loving-kindness is impermanent, [it is not the ultimate].
Thus, the compassion of the śrāvakas uses the unreal to represent the real;
whether their compassion exists or not, it lacks the depth of true pity.
In contrast, the Bodhisattva, abiding in Great Nirvāṇa, uses the real to represent the unreal.
Cultivating this great loving-kindness, one experiences mutual benefit in both waking and dreaming, attaining peace in sleep and wakefulness, being protected by devas and loved by humans.
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"All the contemplations of a bodhisattva are entirely true."
He then said, "In truth, one does not obtain happiness.
Kāśyapa, in this passage, he again raises the second previous question for the Buddha to answer.
The Buddha says, from the following down to "up to the ultimate limit of affection."
The previous second question sought to clarify that the Tathāgata’s compassion aims ultimately at uprooting sentient beings so that they may be freed from suffering and attain peace;
yet, sentient beings themselves are certain to undergo suffering.
For such a person, loving-kindness provides no benefit;
however, for one whose suffering is not fixed,
loving-kindness does provide benefit.
This is the actual fruit of retribution.
The following section, beginning with "Loving-kindness has immeasurable doors," explains why [it is taught].
Although it has been clarified above that loving-kindness and compassion truly bring benefit, it remains unknown who it is that receives this benefit.
From this point onward, it clarifies how nine types of sentient beings obtain benefit therein;
thus, one knows that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is real and not false.
Below, it explains how Bodhisattvas cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy.
The fourth section clarifies the retributive fruits of the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Above, it was clarified that taking loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) as the causes,
one attains the stage of loving one’s children as one’s own as the fruit.
What is meant by "supreme love"?
What is meant by "the only son"? Below are five metaphors;
the first clarifies supreme love.
The latter four similes clarify the "only son.
The simile of seizing the head with the hand and carrying it away represents the prior subduing of afflictions through meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the right hand pulling it out represents the subsequent severance through wisdom (*prajñā*).
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "The words [of the Buddha] are esoteric; based on this, two difficulties arise.
The first difficulty concerns the cause, and the second difficulty concerns the result."
Regarding the first cause, there are three phrases.
If a bodhisattva dwells in the stage of the "only child," it is as when the Tathāgata,
in the past, practiced the bodhisattva path as King Huanyu.
If one regards all sentient beings as an only son, how can one sever the lives of so many Brahmins? How can this be called compassion?
Second, if one has attained the stage of being like an only son, one ought to protect their lives; thus, it is clear that it is impossible to justify the taking of five hundred lives.
Third, if one does not attain [the fruit],
and if one were to take the life of a Brahmin who has not attained even the stage of a "Single-Son" (ekaputraka),
by what cause or condition would one not fall into hell?
If one were to regard those below as equals,
this would be the third difficulty regarding the result;
however, if one regards all sentient beings as one's only child, [there is no such fault].
For what reason did the Tathāgata revile Devadatta as a foolish man who eats snot and spittle,
causing him to give rise to hatred and shed the blood of the Buddha, and why did the Tathāgata further predict his fall into hell?
How does one create the causal conditions for affliction in others?
The World-Honored One, as cited below, uses Subhūti to substantiate the preceding objection that Subhūti is a person of the Hīnayāna.
If he himself observes the minds of sentient beings and does not act as a cause or condition for their afflictions,
how could the Tathāgata act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of Devadatta?
"Suppose a honeybee comes from below"—
this concludes the preceding objections.
From "a honeybee comes" down to "a venomous snake comes," there are seven propositions.
This provides a general answer to the two preceding questions.
From the passage beginning with "poisonous snake" down to "not creating the causal conditions for affliction," there are three phrases;
this is the second admonition.
Regarding what you have said below, this is the third section of the text.
Within the specific responses, first, in answering the first objection, concerning the initial phrase:
"As for your statement that even a Bodhisattva would not intentionally kill a Brahmin."
To clarify that even an ant, though its retribution is in a lowly state, does not intentionally kill because it lacks any path to benefit—
how much more so for a Brahmin,
whose retribution is in a superior state?
How much more so when there is no personal gain in killing?
Rather, it is within one's own fundamental nature that the taking of my life is induced, after which great benefit arises.
Therefore, performing such an act is not called "killing."
From the section on the practice of the *dānapāramitā* onwards,
it is extensively explained how he practiced the six perfections in the past to bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings;
how then could he now again take their lives?
The response to the question asked previously regarding whether this stage was attained corresponds to the second inquiry.
The passage beginning with "At that time, I had already attained" and following answers those who harbor affectionate attachment.

As for the statement "I severed their lives out of great compassion because I felt pity for such beings, as it would have been beneficial," this refers to the compassionate mind, not a malevolent one.
As for that which must be done: the faculties and natures of sentient beings are not uniform;
there may be a single person who, having provoked me, is to be disciplined by my lashings.
Later, when I was about to receive the Way, there was one person who moved me to take my own life;
only then did I undergo transformation. As for others, their faculties and dispositions were such that they responded to my very self;
since I am well-versed in the methods for discerning faculties and dispositions, I must certainly act for their sake.
As for the presence of these three thoughts,
it is truly because I have skillfully recognized his faculties and nature,
providing him with offerings and creating beneficial conditions over twelve years.
The arising of these roots of goodness will cause my life to be cut short;
after my life is cut short, upon witnessing the sufferings of hell, three thoughts of goodness will arise.
By means of the causal conditions of these three thoughts of goodness, one will immediately be born in the Drum of Ambrosia (*Amṛtadundubhi*).
Having attained a lifespan of ten kalpas and successively becoming a sage, there is this great benefit.
How can you say that he was not protected and remembered?
When the killing of Mañjuśrī was completed, many people speculated that he would be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
Regarding the three recollections (*tri-smṛti*), interpretations differ.
According to the present interpretation, this means that when a person’s life ends now and they are about to be born in hell, they have not yet actually entered it.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva, taking this as an object of contemplation, observes the suffering of hell; out of a profound fear of suffering, he gives rise to the three recollections.
One who dies does not possess the form of a hell-being.
At that time, having departed from the human realm, one returns to enter hell.
Upon reaching the edge of hell, one dwells there based on craving; when this body perishes and the time for the arising of nectar arrives, it is called "death."
The passage beginning with "digging the earth and cutting grass" answers the third question:
for what reason do they not fall into hell?
It is because wood and stone are insentient, and a corpse is devoid of life.
Because he harbored an evil intent when he executed punishments such as flogging and whipping,
he incurred sin and fell into hell.
This is intended to clarify that the Tathāgata originally had no evil intent, and therefore has no sin and does not fall into hell.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha as follows:
[He] understood that the Buddha originally had no evil intent and therefore did not fall into hell; why was this so?
It was because he possessed a heart of compassion and a desire to benefit even the smallest ants.
One should truly protect and cherish the lives of sentient beings.
As for why he severed the lives of five hundred Brahmins: it was because he was skilled in knowing causes and conditions;
that is, he was skilled in knowing the faculties, natures, and causal conditions of those Brahmins.
It is precisely appropriate to sever their lives for their benefit.
Those who employ skillful means are well-attuned to the skillful means of transforming things through the eternal.
By means of my mind of skillful means, I sever their lives so that they may plant the seeds of faith in the eternal and in all virtues.
Regarding the killing of ants by the full load of ten carts or less:
this clarifies that those who follow the doctrines of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) calculate merit and demerit based on external objects, asserting that the state of the mind is irrelevant;
thus, they claim that killing ants, tigers, wolves, or even malevolent spirits brings merit and incurs no sin.

If one kills an evil person, although the object of the offense is minor, because the victory over evil is significant, there is sin. To extinguish this and subdue the onset of evil, one should fast for three days and abstain from food;
this is the method for repenting of the offense.
If one kills one's preceptor or ācārya,
this object is most supreme, and one incurs a great offense.
As for women, they are capable of giving birth to all people.
This person is the very root [of society].
If one kills a woman, one cuts off the seed of all people under heaven; thus, this offense is the greatest.
As for the ox, the ox is fundamentally that which plows the fields and cultivates crops to sustain the people.
If one were to kill a cow, even if all the people in the world were to starve to death as a result, it would still constitute a great sin;
yet killing these four persons causes one to fall into the Avīci Hell from which there is no time of escape.
Thus, one knows that there are three kinds of killing.
There are two reasons for treating this separately.
First, the principles of the Buddha-dharma regarding sin and merit do not depend solely on external objects;
they also arise from the mind, which is why one attains hell differently than a non-Buddhist.
Second, those who kill icchantikas from above do not fall;
therefore, [the teaching] arises amidst these three types of killing.
From the smallest ant up to dragons and birds, the retribution for the ten non-virtuous actions constitutes "lower killing," which also leads to falling into hell.
Those who kill from ordinary persons up to those who have attained the stage of *anāgāmin* constitute "middling killing," for they too fall into hell.
One's parents give birth to one’s body and provide nourishment and care; their debt is heavy. Teachers and monks provide instruction and admonition; their kindness is profound.
Those who have attained even a single portion of understanding within the stages of the Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, or the Seed of Practice (śikṣā-bīja) are all termed "definitive bodhisattvas.
These five classes of persons are supreme fields of merit; yet, due to the causal conditions of killing, they undergo the highest sufferings.
One who kills an icchantika has severed their roots of goodness so completely that even though they have committed the act of killing, there is no offense of violating goodness;
whereas killing an animal does entail the offense of violating goodness.
Therefore, they do not fall [into the evil realms].
Among the three types of killing, felling trees and destroying corpses do not constitute any offense that violates goodness.
An icchantika, moreover, possesses no roots of goodness whatsoever.
Because they are like wood or stone, it is said that "it is also thus.
Even if another person were to kill an icchantika, it would not be the case that they do not incur a transgression due to their evil intent;
yet, for one who kills an icchantika, there is no karmic retribution.
The Tathāgata, knowing the capacities of beings from the very beginning, acts for their ultimate benefit; this is called being free from the retribution of sin.
As for what you previously asked—why he reviled Devadatta—[it was for that purpose].
The second point is raised so that the Buddha may respond:

regarding all spoken words being "inconceivable" (acintya), it is intended to clarify that the Tathāgata’s speech is beneficial and not something within the scope of inferior understanding; thus, it is called "inconceivable."
There may be speech that is truthful yet unreasonable, untimely, and unbeneficial to the assembly;
such speech the Buddha does not utter on the path.
There may be speech that is coarse and inappropriate for the occasion; I, too, do not speak such words.
If there is speech that does not accord with human sentiment, it is called coarse and harsh.
Although hearing it is unpleasant, it is not without purpose;
this must necessarily be spoken as a necessary condition for entering the Path.
Why is this so? Because sentient beings awaken to the Way in different ways.

Rāhula spoke these words because he wished to clarify that Devadatta was a person of such stubborn and coarse nature that he could only awaken to the Way through words of stubborn and coarse character; it was for the sake of certainty that he said, "A fool eats saliva."
From "In the wilderness" onwards, it is explained in detail that the Tathāgata’s subduing of stubborn beings is not limited to this single instance.
From "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards, it concerns the realization and understanding [of the teaching].
Just as sugarcane, when repeatedly boiled and processed, yields many kinds of flavors.
I have heard from the Buddha that, as described above, gaining much of the flavor of the Dharma and being able to transcend birth and death is called the "flavor of emergence.
Severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms is called the "flavor of detachment."
To abide constantly in the principle of quiescence is called the "taste of quiescence" (*śānta-rasa*).
That the eternal principle pervades all persons is called the "taste of the path" (*mārga-rasa*).

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "If one cultivates loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy and dwells in the stage of regarding all beings as an only son, what stage does one further attain when cultivating the mind of equanimity?"

The preceding section clarifies that the stage of the "Only Child" (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*), which is the fruit of the three types of practice, takes the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) as its cause; it further addresses what stage is attained next.
The passage beginning with "Excellent! (*sādhu*) provides the answer. There are differing interpretations among scholars regarding this.
From the seventh stage downward, there is the fruit of the householder stage; from the eighth abode upward, there is the fruit of the renunciant stage.
There is another interpretation:
the "Stage of the Single Child" refers to the mind of understanding and practice within the "Nature Stage."
These eleven emptinesses of the night constitute the mind of the first stage.
One who is skilled in knowing the proper time knows that I am now teaching the time of the eleven emptinesses.
Knowing that you wish to ask about what I am about to say,
I have already finished explaining above the fruits of the three types of practitioners;
next, I should explain the fruit of the mind of equanimity.
Your inquiry accords with my own intention. It is as follows:

I shall now speak of the eleven kinds of emptiness; below this, ten people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will hear the Dharma, attain awakening and understanding, and advance in their stages of the Path.
"You have anticipated this point and questioned me accordingly; as it accords with my own mind, I therefore exclaim, 'Excellent!
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is meant by 'emptiness'?"
These form three questions in total:
first, asking about the number of items on the right side of the empty head;
second, asking what kind of dharma is called "empty."
The three questions are explained exclusively within the context of the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, is it not also explained within the context of the eternally abiding True Sovereign (*bhūtārtha*) that emptiness is clarified?
From "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) downward, the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*) is taught; this answers the first head-count, which is the eleventh on the right.
The section on "Absence of Parents" and the aggregates, bases, and elements answers the second question.
Beginning with the ten emptinesses of the *Śālistamba-sūtra*, the eleventh emptiness is distinguished therein.
Based on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the subsequent section clarifies the answer to the third question.
Internal emptiness refers to the category of sentient beings, from those with consciousness at the time of initial conception up to those possessing vajra-bodies; this is called internal emptiness.
The category of insentient things, such as mountains, rivers, trees, and forests, which serve as external phenomena, is called external emptiness.
In the midst of emptiness, there are no parents, enemies, or kin.
Those who conceive of permanence, self, and purity do so through false conceptualizations of permanence, self, and purity.
When one realizes internal emptiness, these sixteen divine selves are eliminated.
The essence of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Saṃgha is truly eternal; that internal phenomena are seen to be impermanent is an external phenomenon.
Furthermore, that which rejects both [impermanence and eternity] is neither internal nor external in nature.
That which is not already present within the body is called "not internal.
That which is not already present but will exist in the future is called "not external.
Why is it neither internal nor external?
Because the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding, it does not reside within internal phenomena.
External emptiness is likewise so.
Previously, in clarifying that the substance of internal phenomena is empty, one set aside external phenomena.
Now, it is explained that external emptiness likewise excludes internal phenomena; this is also the case for the second [type of] emptiness.
Because internal phenomena are designated by names and possess substantial reality, they are empty.

This explains that as for external phenomena such as mountains, why are they called empty because they possess substantial reality? They are empty just like internal phenomena, for there are no internal phenomena [that exist independently].
If one speaks of emptiness as uprooting the fundamental absence of both internal and external,
then by clarifying this with respect to internal and external phenomena, it is called "internal-external emptiness" (adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā). That internal-external emptiness is also like this.

Regarding the third [emptiness], if one begins by observing the internal and external conditioned phenomena separately, it would be difficult to proceed; therefore, after having observed them individually, they are examined together as a unified observation.
For this reason, the third [emptiness] clarifies internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
A certain master explains it thus:
One might think that while the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-Saṃgha may individually be absent within internal and external emptiness, they exist directly when combined.
However, people at that time understood it thus:
since there is no trace of them individually, even when provisionally combined they do not exist; therefore, it is said that internal and external emptiness are likewise so.
The essence of the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is eternally abiding; it does not reside in emptiness, nor does it reside in the conjunction of the third and second [types of] emptiness.
These four dharmas are not termed "empty."
The four dharmas beginning with the Buddha are eternal and wondrously existent; they are not called empty.
As for "both internal and external being empty," this means that both internally and externally there are no dharmas of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha.

Regarding the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): the fourth [emptiness] subsumes the three preceding ones; the phenomena that are the objects of emptiness are precisely one and the same.
When seeking the essence of the conditioned, it is unattainable, and thus all are entirely empty.
This refers to the gates of internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-and-external emptiness.
The terms "permanent," "self," and "pure" indicate the phenomena that are empty.
The dharmas of false conceptualization, from the permanent self up to the life-span, are by nature empty in their original essence.
Even the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, which are dharmas that ought to be eternal, are likewise empty and subject to cessation.
As for the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā):
Furthermore, this Dharma and Sangha may also be called "emptiness in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
It is also said that the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharmatā*), being truly unnameable, is called "emptiness in the ultimate sense."

Among these, that which is called "buddha-nature" refers to the essence of buddha-nature within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which is eternally abiding and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), not a conditioned phenomenon.
Because this buddha-nature is eternal, [it is so called].
"In conditioned emptiness there is no Buddha-nature" concludes the section on conditioned emptiness.
Regarding the contemplation of unconditioned emptiness:
the fifth [point] is that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely empty.
The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are all identical in their emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Space is designated "unconditioned" because it is distinguished by its lack of substantiality, unlike material forms which are produced through conditioning.
From impermanence and suffering up to the internal and external dharmas, the essential nature of these things constitutes the retribution of the three miserable realms.
The state where the retribution of the three miserable realms has been subdued and severed such that it no longer arises is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The state from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward where [defilements] are permanently severed is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
These three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) exist as real entities because they exist in mutual dependence.
Yet, one looks back and finds that these three unconditioned phenomena have been non-existent from the beginning.
Based on these three unconditioned phenomena, emptiness is defined as "unconditioned emptiness.
As for the four dharmas such as the Buddha, they are not conditioned.
Its essence is wondrously distinct from the conditioned existence of birth and death;
yet it is not the unconditioned, for the four dharmas such as the Buddha are primordially present and eternal,
unlike the three types of unconditioned phenomena, which are designated as "unconditioned" only upon the exhaustion of the conditioned.
The essence of Buddha-nature is a wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma;
because it is not [merely] wholesome, it is said that Buddha-nature is wholesome and therefore not unconditioned.
Because its essential nature abides eternally through all time, it is called non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

That which is called "emptiness of the unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā) refers to the emptiness of the four dharmas, such as the Buddha and so forth. "Emptiness of that which is without beginning" (anavarāgra-śūnyatā) refers to...
Sixth, to clarify that sentient beings have, since beginningless time, reckoned in a permanent self:
the Bodhisattva contemplates that all sentient beings since beginningless time are empty.
Those who reckon in a permanent self are merely making arbitrary calculations; from the very beginning, both permanence and self are entirely empty.

The Buddha-nature of the Three Jewels belongs to sentient beings from time immemorial; it is inherently present within their bodies, yet is also empty, for there is no Buddha-nature [as a substantial entity].
As for unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they have likewise existed from time immemorial without being produced by any number of conditions.

It is not a non-conditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma) resulting from analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Therefore, Śāriputra cannot claim that there is no such thing as the unconditioned space-element (ākāśa-asaṃskṛta);
the space-element is eternally present within the bodies of sentient beings.
Furthermore, this correct understanding of beginningless emptiness does not clarify the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, even regarding the three unconditioned phenomena, one must set aside the notion that their nature is empty.

As for the seventh point, most sentient beings cling to the reality of intrinsic nature; thus, the relinquishing of this clinging to intrinsic nature is called "emptiness of nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
Thus far, the six emptinesses have been clarified;
however, people of the time claim that by clarifying emptiness through the negation of phenomena (*vastu*), they take this as the emptiness of phenomena themselves.

Now, to explain the above: the six emptinesses are fundamentally sought as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet such a nature cannot be found; thus they are called "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) rather than "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

From the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) down to the self (*ātman*) and non-self (*anātman*), sentient beings falsely cling to these, asserting them to be real intrinsic natures.
The Bodhisattva contemplates that the original nature is truly unnameable; this is called "emptiness of nature.
As for "emptiness of non-existence," the eighth [category] is the general [classification].
This extensively clarifies internal emptiness and external emptiness.
Human beings are habitually attached to mountains, rivers, trees, and sentient beings, regarding them all as "dharmas belonging to me.
How can these be categorically empty? The Tathāgata understands your calculations.
All phenomena are fundamentally without seeking; because they cannot be named as "having," they are called "non-existence" (anupalabdhi) and "emptiness.

There is another interpretation: while the Tathāgata previously clarified the seven types of emptiness primarily in terms of objective spheres (*viṣaya*), this eighth [emptiness] is explained primarily in terms of the subject.
To define "emptiness" as "that which is non-existent" is precisely what is meant by emptiness;
one need not inquire whether it is conditioned or unconditioned, for all things are non-existent, and thus it is called "universal.
When the Great Being contemplates this non-existence:
All phenomena are utterly swept away, like a destitute person;
this is what is meant by "all is empty.
As for the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā):
The ninth [section], "Supreme Illumination," clarifies that non-existence is empty and transcends all provisional designations and deceptions.
At that time, people cling to the notion of a singular self;
now, the dharma of emptiness exists, yet it is not like a pillar, for it is that which is entrusted to the minds of the noble ones.
Now, if one directly analyzes the nature of things, since the sickness is empty, it should be called "the emptiness of emptiness.

This corresponds to the tenth [type of emptiness], the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), found in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Therefore, it is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
First the substantial dharmas are explained, and subsequently the provisional designations are explained.
When this eye arises, there is nothing from which it comes;
there is not a single eye that exists.
From the future to the present—
this clarifies that the future is empty.
Furthermore, as for "having gone nowhere," it means that the actual eye does not enter the past.
This clarifies that the emptiness of the past is due to conditions not yet having met; it is called "originally non-existent" because the meeting of conditions has not occurred.

This explains that the emptiness of the future is due to present conditions meeting, hence it is called "already existing"; when conditions depart, it is called "non-existent," which is explained as returning to non-existence.

The past is empty; in its provisional and ultimate nature, it has no eye and no master, and is thus called the "emptiness of the present. Since the visual faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*) is empty across the three periods of time, the remaining faculties are likewise so.
As for the existence of karma and its retribution:
The statement that "provisional names exist" reveals that the practitioner of the contemplation of emptiness does not perceive a creator;
this proceeds from the coarse to the subtle.
Why is it that the real dharmas are explained first, followed by the provisional names?
The commentary states:
This refers to the time [of realization], not the time of practice.

The tenth "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) is the eternally abiding ultimate truth; it is precisely the point where the followers of the Two Vehicles become deluded regarding the two [truths].
That which exists is the eternally abiding wondrous Way;
that which does not exist is the eternally abiding wondrous non-existence.
This is termed the "emptiness of emptiness," which is a fetter.
Regarding the principle of "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*):

when people hear it said that all phenomena are empty, they either claim it is an existence like that of birth and death, or they claim it is a non-existence like the voidness of nature prior to the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*). To cling to existence or cling to non-existence is to fail to comprehend the principle; this is what is called the "emptiness of emptiness."
"This is this" refers to the affirmative phrase of the existence of birth-and-death;
"this is not this" refers to the negative phrase of the emptiness of nature.
It is neither "this is this" nor "this is not this," which is the negative phrase of the emptiness of nature.
"Neither-is-nor-is" refers to the double negation.
The essence of eternally abiding nirvana is a wondrous existence;
it is not the existence of saṃsāra.
Its essence is wondrous non-existence;
it is not the non-existence of the emptiness of arising.
To transcend both existence and non-existence is what is called "emptiness of emptiness."
Furthermore, the Master explains that "it exists" and "it does not exist" refers to wondrous existence and wondrous non-existence, which transcend the provisional existence of conditions.
Because its essence is severed and its nature is empty of existence, it is called "emptiness of emptiness.
The repetition of "is" and "is" (是是) raises both [terms] in order to subsequently negate them both.
The first "is" refers back to the previously mentioned "wondrous existence."
First, it is called "wondrously non-arising" (miao wulai).

When people hear that there is something produced, they certainly have a mental intention to go and grasp it; when they hear that there is nothing produced, they certainly have no mental intention to go and grasp it.
That which is "not this" is not identical to "this"; it is neither identical nor non-identical, and is without action.
Even if one were determined to go and grasp it, one could not bring it about.
It is definitively neither something that can be grasped by going toward it, nor is its essence obtainable.
This wondrous existence and wondrous non-existence have never been the same as worldly things;
the attachments of existence and non-existence within the mind are utterly severed.
The emptiness of emptiness refers to the fact that even the grasping at the definite existence or non-existence of things is empty; it is called the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness.
This is not the same as the realm and wisdom of the two vehicles, wherein both the object and the cognition are equally empty.
The ten emptinesses are the external objects;
this clarifies the internal contemplation of the mind.
While the mind is established as having the reality of the three characteristics, when viewed from the perspective of its essence, it is empty.
In this contemplation, the mind illuminates the two truths such that all phenomena are utterly cleared away;
being equal to empty space, it is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).
This refers to [the merit] from ten Ganges Rivers downward.
The preceding section clarified the eleven kinds of emptiness;
this [section] demonstrates the attainment of benefits. As for the passage beginning with "also seeing and also knowing," why has this text been introduced here?
The above clarifies that the Bodhisattva attained the realization of the eleven emptinesses within the midst of space.
At that time, people conceived doubts, thinking:
"How can one attain the realization of the eleven emptinesses within the midst of space?"
Within existence there is nothing further to be known.
The Tathāgata is the Great Being who descends [to this world];
not only does he attain the eleven types of emptiness within emptiness, but he also attains the understanding of emptiness.
Within this middle stage, one further attains eight knowledges, insights,
and awakenings. Furthermore, there is another master who explains that the Great Being (Mahāsattva) attains the realization of the eleven emptinesses within emptiness.
Once the understanding of emptiness is clear and distinct,
one will certainly be able to illuminate existence with clarity and achieve thorough mastery of emptiness; furthermore,
by recognizing existence and understanding emptiness, and by comprehending existence, one becomes capable of examining and transforming those who can be guided.
Therefore, there are eleven kinds of emptiness.
Following this, the eight types of knowledge, vision, and awakening are explained.
From here on, the eight kinds of knowledge and vision are explained in general.
First, he answers by providing a general explanation of the causes and conditions of practice regarding right view.
Second, from the passage on self-starvation downward, he explains how wrong views regarding causes lead to the attainment of pleasant fruits.
Third, seeing that sentient beings initially practice wrong causes, he demonstrates that their end will be correct.
The fourth [point] clarifies knowledge and vision by means of the medicinal teachings on permanent and impermanent phenomena.
The fifth clarifies knowledge and vision by following the flow of both the contrary and the conforming, based on knowing the faith of these sentient beings.
The sixth [section], from "seeing all sentient beings cultivate their bodies or mental wisdom" onwards,
proceeds by transforming karma to clarify knowledge and vision.
The seventh [section], from "knowing that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature" onwards...
Regarding the clear knowledge and vision of the Buddha-nature,
there are three parts within this.
First, it clarifies that those in the nine stages of abiding know [the Buddha-nature] but do not see it.
Next, it is explained that those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) know but see little.
Third, it is explained that the Tathāgata both knows and sees.
From the eighth section, beginning with "so-called worldly letters," and so forth.
Based on the two truths of emptiness and existence, one clearly understands through insight;
this constitutes the practice that initiates subsequent fruition,
with the auxiliary retribution serving as its condition.
Internally there is the unchanging nature of names;
externally there are the manifesting characteristics of names and forms.
Because they are non-existent yet serve as the causes for the discernment of existence, and because they are distant, they are called conditions (*pratyaya*).
If sentient beings possess the three kinds of mind— wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral— they can give rise to that which is called "existence," which has its roots in the faculties.
One who practices meditative concentration knows right concentration and wrong concentration.
That which carries one across is called a vehicle (*yāna*).
A Bodhisattva is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);
those of the two vehicles are not true spiritual friends.
It is called "precept" (*śīla*) because it stops evil.
If the giver knows that they exist while practicing giving with signs,
yet knows that they will cease to exist within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) while practicing giving without signs, they will realize *nirvāṇa*.

Eighth, regarding the source from which knowledge and vision arise: since it was stated among the ten preceding emptinesses that there is "no knowledge and no vision," people at that time conceived a doubt,
thinking that the essence of the eleven emptinesses must be existent, profound, and identical to Suchness (tathatā).
Because the Buddha-nature is profound, it cannot be seen.
Even when one is about to depart [from this world], if the mind conceives that the Buddha-nature is a wondrous existence,
it is because of its extreme profundity that those from the ninth stage downward do not see it at all.
Because the essence of the preceding eleven emptinesses is non-existent, they are not seen;
it is not because they are profound that they are said to lack knowledge and vision.
For this reason, the eighth passage arises.
Just as the names and functions of groves and vehicles exist conventionally such that they are both known and seen,
when viewed from the perspective of ultimate reality, because groves and vehicles do not exist and are empty, it is clarified that there is neither knowing nor seeing.
Furthermore, there is the knowledge of what is bestowed as a gift.
This is the ninth successive reason for being born in the superior groves of the Radiant Heaven (*Ābhāsvara*) with celestial chariots;
this is called "possessing both application, as well as knowledge and vision."
At that time, the assembly again gave rise to doubt and attachment, thinking that there must truly exist dharmas that give rise to human cognition and views, which in turn produce the mind.

[The Buddha replied: "In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there is wisdom, giving, and meditative concentration; these are called 'existent by function' (yǒngyǒu), not 'existent in reality' (shíyǒu)."
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are no names such as giving, hearing, or wisdom; this returns to the eighth point mentioned previously.
That the Bodhisattva knows these eight kinds is the same understanding as that known by the Tathāgata’s five eyes; this concludes the verse.
The fourth section on the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) constitutes the third major division.
As for why these are explained after the eleven emptinesses and the eight types of knowledge and vision:
the preceding section has already established the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) as the cause.
These four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) constitute the fruit.
Regarding the statement that the treatise on the fruit contains ten million words,
it refers only to the essentials within the ten thousand practices (sahasra-caryā).
The superior directly clarifies that one must be skilled in knowing emptiness while simultaneously being skilled in knowing existence.
The inferior examines and transforms beings; such skillful transformation of people requires the essential possession of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Therefore, Kāśyapa asked:
The Bodhisattva thus knows the eleven kinds of emptiness and the eight kinds of knowledge and vision.
What further benefit does he subsequently obtain?
The Buddha spoke as follows in response.
This refers to the benefit of transforming others through the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) attained subsequent to realization.
Within these four unimpeded knowledges, there are generally six sections for explanation;
the first section elucidates the four unimpeded knowledges by way of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
The second section, from "the Bodhisattva’s universal knowledge" down to "śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas," clarifies the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) by way of the three vehicles.
The third section, from "non-attachment" onwards, clarifies the four analytical knowledges by way of their meaning (*artha*).

The fourth section, from "The Bodhisattva’s Skillful Knowledge of the Retention of Syllables" (*akṣara-dhāraṇī*) onwards, clarifies the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) by means of analogies.
The fifth section, from "Immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas" onwards, clarifies that the Great Being has long planted the causes for them and is fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges.
Those who have transcended the two vehicles do not possess the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the sixth point, Kāśyapa asks, "How is it that Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom? and so forth; this section serves to reconcile [the teachings] with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
The Dharma is without obstruction throughout the world; that which neither arises nor is non-arising, neither form nor mind, yet possesses a patterned function, is called "Dharma.
Not being attached to this Dharma is called "unobstructed regarding the Dharma.
The nature of permanence and impermanence is empty; all phenomena are therefore termed "names" and "meanings."
Within this, not being attached to names or meanings is the unimpeded [knowledge] of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
As for "phrases" (*nirukti*), it refers to the ability to purify the gardens of eloquence and to have one's virtuous renown heard in other regions;
within this, not being attached to names or phrases is the unimpeded [knowledge] of phrasing (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

"Pleasant speech" (*pratibhāna*) means that the mind has a longing for and reverence toward [the Dharma], which is called "pleasure" (*prati*); to explain and disperse [doubts] for others is called "speech" (*bhāna*).
To be without attachment therein is the unimpededness of pleasant speech (*pratibhānā-pratighāta*).
One who knows all phenomena (*dharma*) as well as the names of those phenomena—
The twelve divisions of the sūtras, both eternal and impermanent,
as well as mountains, pillars, beams, and all other things that possess functional utility, are called "Dharma. Within these,
one does not become attached to names or dharmas, remaining unimpeded.
"To know all phenomena" means to know that the myriad phenomena have their basis, just as a pillar has the function of supporting;
it is the meaning of establishing names according to phenomena, wherein the myriad phenomena are likewise so. This is the meaning of "name and meaning."
Regarding *nirukti* (etymological interpretation): it is to understand the meaning according to the characters and to extract the meaning from within the sounds.

Even worldly discourse involves these four types of analysis; among these, when one frequently encounters excellent speech and sound, and masters them therein, this constitutes the unimpeded mastery of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding "delight in preaching":
