May we all take refuge in the Tathāgata, who teaches the Dharma according to our faculties and forever severs the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), thereby skillfully extracting the poisoned arrows.
The physicians of the world treat illness with difficulty; though they may temporarily subdue it and bring about recovery, the disease inevitably returns.

The Tathāgata uses the medicines of permanence and impermanence to treat the illnesses of sentient beings—such as the single poison and its like—so that they are eradicated forever and never arise again.

[The passage] beginning with "He said to the Buddha" constitutes the third section, which seeks to cause the Tathāgata to manifest his precepts, concentration, wisdom, knowledge, vision, and awakening.
First, regarding those who do not know or see according to worldly standards:
if a Bodhisattva were one who knows and sees, he would not say that what the world does not know is known by the Great Being.
If this were so, what would be the distinguishing characteristic of this Bodhisattva’s practice compared to that of worldly beings?
The Buddha spoke as follows in response:
"As for what you asked regarding how this differs:
if there is a person who hears [this teaching] and maintains faith from beginning to end,"
These worldly bodhisattvas are likewise like ordinary people in that they do not know the Buddha-nature;
yet these bodhisattvas are those who have attained knowledge, vision, and awakening,
cultivating the cause of the practice of pure precepts and signlessness.
This is knowing, seeing, and awakening; it is the bodhisattva’s understanding that transcends the world.

By these causes and conditions, this is the cause and condition for purifying the precepts through the extinction of marks; in every place of birth, one constantly maintains the purity of the precepts through the extinction of marks.
When the precepts are already pure, one ultimately perceives the Buddha-nature; this is called "purity.
Understanding that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, one never says that the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa.
Next, regarding the cultivation of meditative concentration: the precepts originally serve to prevent wrongdoing.
Following the sublime precepts, one next cultivates superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Tranquility" refers to the mind of principle and the mind of right concentration together severing and eliminating erroneous thoughts;
thus it is said that "right mindfulness does not forget."
In the tranquil mind of principle, one constantly proclaims that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
To take meditative concentration as the cause and thereby attain the eleven kinds of emptiness is true wisdom.
Next, regarding the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*): following the sublime concentration (*samādhi*), one subsequently gives rise to the correct contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) of the Middle Way.
For one who cultivates wisdom, the understanding of the Middle Way ultimately has something to be eliminated; what is it that is eliminated? It is the sixteen types of *ātman*.
Regarding the view that the self is within the body: this refers to cases where the body is large and the self is small, such as [the analogy of] a lamp inside a grain of rice or a bean.
Regarding the view that the body is within the self: this refers to the self being large while the body does not pervade it; it is the divine self (*ātman*) that pervades all places.
"To say 'this is me' is to conceive of the self based on the aggregates (*skandha*).
To say 'neither body nor self' is to conceive of the self apart from the aggregates.
This refers to the six aspects of maintaining the precepts, beginning with "this is the removal of what is to be discarded; the mind is free from regret."
Next, one cultivates the supreme samādhi, wherein the myriad practices mutually support one another;
ultimately, one perceives the Buddha-nature, clearly realizing that no marks remain.
Hereafter follows another interpretation.
"From 'the precepts one has received are firm and unshakable' onwards,
the first cycle above clarifies how the myriad practices for attaining Bodhi assist one another, ultimately leading to the realization of Buddha-nature and the severance of the mundane world."
From this point onward, it is clarified that the pure precepts of a bodhisattva dwelling in the higher stages serve as the cause.
Through principle, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is aroused;
following concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) naturally arises.
Having perfected the practices of the ten stages and clearly perceived the Buddha-nature to attain Great Nirvana,
such is the supramundane bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa asked: "What is meant by 'practicing and upholding the pure precepts'?

The intent of the question was: how can it be that worldly bodhisattvas, while permitted to practice the precepts according to their own methods, are unable to thereby bring forth the myriad practices?

How does a world-transcending Mahāsattva permit the application of dharmas through the cultivation of the provision of precepts to initiate various practices and attain the vision of the Buddha-nature?
The intent of these two questions is that for a worldly Bodhisattva, the beginning and end of cultivating the precepts mutually support one another until the ultimate Buddha-nature is realized.
How can one say that [the person] spoken of is a Great Being who has transcended the world?
Good son, as for the meaning of the answer below: worldly precepts take the three realms as their goal and result, thereby increasing birth and death.
Therefore, when the myriad practices do not mutually support one another, one does not perceive the Buddha-nature;
this is called worldly precept.
As for your previous question regarding how the application of dharmas in the cultivation of precepts ultimately leads to the perception of the Buddha-nature: [it is as follows].

To clarify that the Mahāsattva observes the precepts while transcending all marks—neither anticipating the retributive fruits of the three realms of existence nor relying on the mutual support of the myriad practices to finally perceive the Buddha-nature—it is said that "the precepts are not precepts.
Within the practice of the Way, observing the precepts to prevent wrongdoing is what is called "precepts."
Within the path of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), all phenomena are utterly swept away.
Since there is no precept to be cultivated, it is called "non-precept," and thus it can be termed the "precept of signs.
When one attains the precept of signlessness (*animitta-śīla*), the precept of grasping at signs is severed; this is called "precept as non-precept."
That which is non-conditioned does not expect the three realms of existence; thus, upholding the precepts is called "non-conditioned.
Because the mind that understands signlessness is ultimate, upholding these pure precepts and bestowing them upon sentient beings is called "arising."
This is the concluding statement regarding the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.
Following the pure precepts, the bodhisattva does not direct the mind toward the loss [of virtue] nor feel regret;
rather, they simply take the absence of such signs as the cause for maintaining [the precepts].
A mind free from regret arises spontaneously.
When the adamantine mind of the tenth stage subsides, one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature and attains Great Nirvana;
such a person is no longer of the mundane world.
It is like a person holding a mirror;
this serves as an analogy for observing the precepts.
Just as a person holding a mirror does not see their own face, yet the reflection of the face appears of its own accord.
When a lamp is lit, it does not extinguish darkness; rather, the darkness is naturally extinguished.
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one does not intentionally think, "I am producing the second stage";
it is simply for the sake of the first stage that the second stage arises naturally.
The same applies to the ten lower stages.
From the passage "A person of upright appearance sees their own reflection" onwards,
[the text] provides analogies for those who maintain the precepts and those who violate them.
As for the two women tending cattle:
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra in twenty-five thousand verses is the cattle;
those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them are the two women.
One person held a jar of fermented grain-drink;
the drink is a metaphor for upholding the precepts.
Another person held a jar of curd.
The metaphor of the curd represents the breaking of the precepts.
"Arriving together at the city" means arriving together at the city of Great Nirvana.
As for "those who wish to sell":
cultivating the causes to purchase the fruit is called "selling.
Regarding "on the road": the Eightfold Noble Path is called the "road."
"Falling" refers to the exhaustion of past karma;
"both jars breaking" refers to the passing away of the two individuals' subtle bodies.
First, the "joyful one" is likened to a jar of gruel that originally contained curd; because one desired to obtain butter, it was strained.
Although the jar later broke after the butter was obtained, the resulting gruel and oil were not to be regretted. This is a metaphor for maintaining the precepts to give rise to true understanding.
This is called "joy" because the passing away of the body is not yet to be regretted.
As for "sorrow," it refers to when one was originally storing milk to seek to obtain butter;
failing to obtain it during the interim while the jar remained empty is a profound cause for regret. This serves as a metaphor for the precepts with signs (*saṃskṛta-śīla*).
One cannot give rise to the fruits of the noble ones (*āryaphala*).
"This body having perished, one falls into the three miserable realms" refers to sorrow (*śoka*).
"Whether observing the precepts or violating them is likewise" serves as a metaphor.
Regarding the distinction between joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*): Kāśyapa asked about the differentiation between these two mental factors.
When one sits upright and refrains from evil, it is called joy;
when one maintains pure precepts and is certain of attaining the realm of nirvāṇa, it is called bliss.
The second contemplation, observing arising as non-arising, is called joy (*muditā*);
seeing the great *nirvāṇa* at the time of its realization is called bliss (*sukha*).
Regarding the third phrase, that which is below is called joy, and that which is above is called bliss.
The fourth is called joy (*prīti*) because it is free from the common dharmas of birth and death;
it is called bliss (*sukha*) when one attains the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
The fifth is called joy because, by upholding the precepts, one eliminates the ten unwholesome actions.
Clearly perceiving the Buddha-nature at the time of attaining pure liberation is called bliss.
"Not of the world" is the concluding phrase.
That which constitutes the body through five factors are: faith, shame, remorse, a spiritual friend, and reverence for the precepts.
These five dharmas that provoke the inquiry for *nirvāṇa* are called the "reliances" (*niśraya*).
To be free from the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) means to realize the reality of all phenomena; to sever and eliminate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is called "separation.

Regarding the five doubts: the first is doubt concerning the Three Jewels as to whether they exist or not; the second is doubt regarding the precepts; the third is doubt regarding non-heedlessness (*apramāda*). This [state] should correspond to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
Hearing [the Dharma] constantly gives rise to understanding and severs the five doubts.
One who attains the five faculties (pañcendriya) is one whose faith can produce nirvāṇa; thus, it is called a "faculty" (indriya), as is the case with the following four.
Regarding the five kinds of nirvāṇa: the point at which the afflictions of grasping at the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are exhausted is called the five kinds of nirvāṇa.
This is not mundane morality.
If my disciples recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* down to the passage, "How could one not receive and uphold it until the next life? this clarifies that they possess no [mundane] precepts.
My disciples must be careful not to treat this with levity or mockery.
From the passage "Since they have not been my disciples" onwards,
it clarifies that there is no fixed [status];
from "Those who receive and uphold this sutra are not speaking at an improper time" onwards, [it clarifies that they are].
At this time, when the retinues of Māra arrive, they will think, "This is without wisdom; it should not be circulated in this way.
When my disciples receive and uphold this sutra, [they shall encounter such obstacles].
First, by violating the prohibitive precepts, one causes the sutra to lack power and majesty,
leading immeasurable sentient beings to slander and disbelieve it.
Second, one causes the sutra to lack power and majesty.
Third, one must not cause others to copy or paint [the image] correctly.
Fourth, it causes people to fall into hell.
Fifth, it prevents people from attaining the fruits of rebirth as humans or devas.
Therefore, one should not uphold my sutra.
If my disciples who uphold this sutra maintain the prohibitive precepts,
it will first cause the sutra to possess awesome power.
Second, to cause them to receive and uphold [the teachings] so that they may be correctly transcribed and correctly illustrated;
third, to cause them not to slander [them];
fourth, to cause people not to fall into hell.
Fifth, it causes people to obtain the fruits of human and celestial realms in the near term, and to attain eternal bliss in the distant future.
These three types of persons uphold my Dharma.
When one wishes to uphold it:
One must maintain right mindfulness within the mind and not be frivolous or restless.
Teaching the Dharma at the appropriate time gives rise to right view in people;
if one teaches it at an inappropriate time, it gives rise to wrong view in people.
Therefore, it is said that there is nothing that should not be spoken at the proper time and nothing that should not be schemed for.
Within other lands where the Hinayana is believed and practiced, one may not preach the sutras on permanence; if one were to preach them, it would give rise to false views in others.
Regarding those who do not request instruction, one must insistently request it three times before teaching them;
furthermore, one must not teach others on an improper occasion alone. Why is this so?
If one's life has been meager and narrow, the sutras will lack power.
The same applies to the following phrase.
This is when one wishes to preach the sutras or speak of the Buddha-nature.
First, one must maintain pure precepts; the purification of body, mind, and speech is called "purity of body.
Second, one cultivates meditative concentration to eliminate restlessness and agitation.
Third, at the appropriate time, one develops supreme wisdom to eliminate false views.
If one speaks even a single phrase or a single verse to cause another to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta,
then such a person is a true spiritual friend and my disciple.

Furthermore, "Good son, all those in the world do not know or perceive" refers to the fourth assembly, where the arising of understanding through the six recollections is called knowledge, vision, and perception (*jñāna-darśana-bodha*).

Recollecting the Buddha is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), wherein these four [recollections] are absent; these four are matters pertaining to the fruit, while precepts and giving are practices pertaining to the cause.
How is it that the Tathāgata is explained as coming for the three reasons?
The Buddhas of the past taught the twelve divisions of the sūtras to transform sentient beings;
the Tathāgata does likewise.
He expounds the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
because he is as the Buddha has taught, he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, because he has attained Great Nirvāṇa through the six pāramitās and the eleven kinds of emptiness—the fundamental vehicle of the Buddhas—he is called the Tathāgata.
In the past, the Buddhas of the three periods of existence opened up the three vehicles to save sentient beings;
their lifespans were immeasurable.
The Tathāgata is likewise.
Just as the Buddhas of the past benefited sentient beings through the three vehicles and possessed an actual lifespan that was immeasurable, they were called Tathāgatas.
What is meant by "Arhat"?
Generally, there are five ways to explain this term.
The world does not say that all dharmas are enemies because the Buddha should destroy them; rather, it is called "correspondence" (*yoga*) because it accords with the eight provisional principles.
Second, the four Māras are fundamentally firm in their disordering of practitioners.
This Bodhisattva is called "Worthy" (Arhat) because, while on the stage of a Buddha’s causal ground, he should destroy the four māras;
he is called "Worthy" because, at the time of being a Bodhisattva, he should sever and abandon all afflictions.

Fourth, when Bodhisattvas were on the stage of practice, they should undergo suffering for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable eons; because their bodies and minds were always joyful, they are called "Responsive" (*yìng*).
Fifth, the Buddhas now currently exist and should receive the flowers, incense, food, and drink offered by humans; thus they are called "Responsive."
The preceding section is explained based on the true state (*tathatā*);
the subsequent one is explained with respect to the responsive Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Regarding the question "What is the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*)?", there are generally four ways of explaining it.
"Right" (samyak) refers to the eternally abiding principle; because it is free from error, it is called "right.

"Omniscient" (sarvajña) means that regarding the non-erroneous nature of permanence, bliss, suffering, impermanence, and so forth, there is nothing that is not thoroughly understood; thus it is called "Right Omniscience" (samyaksambuddha).

Second, regarding the ascetic who correctly practices the water-dwelling austerity: if one merely observes equal precepts, one will fully know that the practice of asceticism yields the retributive fruits of the three miserable realms; this is the full knowledge of the causes and effects of asceticism.
The third is the principle within the mundane world regarding correct names.
As for "knowing," it means that by knowing how to cultivate and concentrate upon the Middle Way, one attains the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
The fourth "correct" refers to the stage prior to the Vajra [stage], which can indeed be numbered and measured.
The "All-Knowing One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) is so named because after knowing the vajra-like [wisdom], that which is incalculable and immeasurable is fully known.

If one speaks of the two vehicles, although they also possess "all-knowing" regarding the realms and sense-bases, they do not exhaustively know the underlying principle; therefore, it is not the same as the All-Knowing One.
What is meant by "one perfected in knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*)?
There are five general explanations.
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the three types of higher knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*) within the state of fruition.
The practitioner is so named because they rely on the vehicle of causes—precepts and wisdom—and thereby conjoin with the fruit; this is called "perfection of conduct" (*caryā-pāda*).

Later, it is explained that the perfection of conduct is the essence of the Tathāgata. Because his conduct is fully perfected, he is called one who has attained the perfection of knowledge and conduct (*vidyā-caryā-sampanna*).
Regarding the "Three Clarities" (trividyā) as explained from the perspective of the fruition:
first, the "clarity of a bodhisattva" refers to the mind of the Great Way within the state of fruition, and not that of the lower stages.
Second, regarding "the illumination of all Buddhas":
the Buddha’s illumination thoroughly penetrates the three periods of time. Regarding "non-illumination and illumination": [it refers to the fact that] there is no illumination.
The absence of dharma and ignorance is called "the light of non-light.
Regarding the term "Sugata," there are generally three interpretations:
"Gata" means "gone," "one who has gone by means of the Great Nirvāṇa," or "one who transforms sentient beings."
Regarding the second point, concerning those who enter nirvana with a mind skilled in the vehicle:
the answer is that although one reaches the state of nirvāṇa where names and characteristics do not exist, names and characteristics are spoken of for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Regarding the term "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*), there are generally five interpretations.
One who thoroughly understands the causes and effects of good and evil within the world, and understands the world itself, is called a "Knower of the World.
Regarding the term "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), there are also generally five interpretations.
Humans and devas are superior beings (*uttama-puruṣa*).
A single Buddha is the unsurpassed being (*anuttara-puruṣa*), beyond whom there is none higher.
Therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Being.
The essence of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is the most supreme, with nothing superior to it; thus they are called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).
Regarding the term "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*), there are generally three interpretations:
the Tathāgata is himself a man, and furthermore, he is the tamer of men.
The title "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām) has three general interpretations.
A teacher possesses the grace of instruction, while a disciple possesses the duty of reverent inquiry.
Because he is able to transform and provide for both humans and gods, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
The Buddha acts as a teacher for animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth;
however, since humans and devas are the primary recipients of the Way, he speaks here specifically to them.
A Buddha is called "Buddha" because he has awakened himself and awakens others.
He is called Bhagavat because he has destroyed the afflictions (*kleśa*).
From the passage "Whether man or woman" onwards, the preceding section concludes the exposition on the Buddha; from here below, there is the exhortation to have faith.
Why is this passage introduced here at the end of the immeasurable eons?
By what means were the fruits of the ten titles [of the Buddha] previously mentioned attained?
This is truly because, throughout immeasurable kalpas, one made offerings to one's parents and clarified the four immeasurable minds as the cause;
thus, one attains the fruit of the ten titles mentioned above.
As for the supramundane mind:
As for the origin of these fifty minds:
they truly arise because one practiced these fifty minds during the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).
Therefore, one has attained the resultant realm of the ten epithets (*daśa-nāmadheya*) as described above.
One who knows the mind knows the distinction between the realms of the permanent and the impermanent.
One who knows the realm of arising knows that the arising mind exists within the permanent and the impermanent.
One who knows the mind of abiding in the realm...
The mind constantly abides in the realm of the permanent and the impermanent, knowing their middle.
Regarding the knowledge of the mind within the realm of mastery (*vaśitā*):
the contemplation that allows it to be relaxed and released is called "mastery."
Therefore, because one has previously made offerings to one's parents and cultivated the four immeasurables and fifty mental states,
one causes them to attain the fruit of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the three types of mindfulness: first, one listens to the Dharma with a single mind, neither rejoicing when hearing it nor feeling sorrow when not hearing it;
second, whether people come or go, one constantly practices the practice of equanimity.
These three objects give rise to the foundations of mindfulness; thus they are called the "three foundations of mindfulness.
That which is mindful of phenomena refers to the eternally abiding Dharma, which enables sentient beings to attain manifest results.
By recollecting the causes and conditions of the Dharma, one attains the fruit of renown in the present and may also attain the stage of practice.
Regarding "there being no fixed time," this means that in transforming others through the eternal Dharma, there is no restriction of time.
Furthermore, the eternal dharma (*nityadharma*) is not subject to temporal limitations.
This eternal dharma is that which is perceived by the Dharma-eye, not by the fleshly eye.
It is not the case that what was originally non-existent comes to have a name, nor does it arise through birth.
That which was previously existent and subsequently becomes non-existent is called "non-emergence.
In the case of eternal dharmas, there is neither abiding nor cessation.
For that which has no dwelling place, as with eternal dharmas, there is neither arising nor a dwelling place.
As for those who act as providers of dwellings:
according to the constant law, they manifest impermanence through the frost and dew that affect the practitioner, yet they name it a "dwelling.
To people, they act as permanent teachers and supports, yet they lack clear understanding regarding sentient beings.
It is able to provide a great illumination for humans and devas.
It enables people to reach the eternal shore.
It grants humans the eternal, unimpeded fragrance that severs all worldly pleasures.
It is the severance of the pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) among the three feelings.
Its essence is eternally termed "tranquility" (*kṣema*).
Its essence is beyond the four realms of existence (*catur-gati*), and is thus called the "other shore" (*pāra*).
That which is not form is not the form of the lower stages;
having completely severed all form of the lower stages,
this form manifests its essential substance.
This refers to its wondrous form (*rūpa*), which can correctly be said to be neither karma nor fetters (*saṃyojana*);
yet it cannot be said that it is not karma or fetters, for karma and fetters are fundamentally dharmas of the lower stages (*adhobhūmi*).
As for "not being a thing," it means it is not a thing of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
That which severs things severs the things of the lower stages;
yet this [entity] is a permanently abiding thing.
That which is not of the realms is not of the realms of birth and death of the lower stages.
One who enters the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) abandons all realms of the lower stages;
yet this "realm" is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The remaining phrases are to be understood in the same manner.
That which is not the teaching is called "not the teaching" because its principle transcends words;
yet manifesting forms in the world is not itself "not the teaching.
One who is a teacher is called a "teacher" because they are able to bring about the state of a sage.
"Non-ceasing" refers to the fact that its essence transcends the stages below;
thus it is called "non-ceasing.
"Not non-ceasing" means that for the sake of sentient beings, it manifests as being identical to the cessation of the lower stages, yet it cuts off all cessation of those lower stages.
This "stopping" (*śamatha*) is the sublime concentration within the fruit.
What is meant by "recalling the Sangha"?
Its essence is eternally abiding and cannot be grasped, yet it is able to produce the field of merit for sentient beings.

Although it serves as a field of merit, although it gives rise to blessings within the minds of sentient beings, its essence is devoid of marks and names; thus, it is called "without receiving or grasping.
Its essence is free from all burdens; thus, it is called "pure and undefiled. Its principle transcends conceptual deliberation; thus, it is called "vast and boundless."
What is the mindfulness of precepts?
It is to contemplate that one possesses the precepts without violation;
this is the essence of the Mahāyāna precepts.
That which is not a physical obstruction is called "non-distinct.
Because it can restrain the evils of beings, it is called "capable of being guarded and maintained.
Practicing this precept enables one to attain nirvana; thus, it is called the "cause" of the precepts.
It enables practitioners to give birth to the name "Vessel" within the ocean of non-arising;
it adorns practitioners with the name "Necklace";
and it causes people to attain Buddhahood, named "Great Nature."
That which benefits all things is called the great ocean;
that which can remove the defilements of human afflictions is called lye;
and that which provides shelter from frost and dew is called a dwelling.
That which can sever the afflictions is called a sword;
that which enables the practitioner to cross over birth and death is called a bridge;
that which cures the disease of the afflictions is called a skilled physician.
That which enables practitioners to reach the great fruit by means of this is called the feet;
that which removes the darkness of human ignorance and gives rise to the understanding of human wisdom and illumination is called the eyes;
and that which removes the heat of afflictions is called the cool shade.
It can cause people to ascend the ladder to nirvana.
If one abides in this precept, it is the precept of the Hīnayāna;
if one abides in the Hīnayāna precepts, one may also attain the four fruits of the śrāvaka.
However, I do not maintain the Mahāyāna precepts with the expectation that I shall ultimately attain nirvāṇa.
What is meant by "mindfulness of giving"?
It is when a Great Being practices giving without attachment to signs and thereby ultimately attains the fruit of bodhi.
If one does not practice giving, one will ultimately not attain Buddhahood;
how then could one adorn the fourfold assembly in the future?
It is precisely by practicing giving without attachment to signs that one attains Buddhahood in the future and is able to adorn the fourfold assembly.
If one is my disciple,
as described above in its distinct aspects,
this constitutes the six recollections.
In brief, the correct and singular Dharma-recollection consists of practicing the twelve divisions of the scriptures of the Hīnayāna.
To say that it is no different from the present *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is incorrect.
When speaking these words, what intention was intended? It was to obstruct the sutras and to claim that the profound ancient sutras are inferior.
This present sutra is supreme.
The phrase "How marvelous! How wondrous! and those that follow are praises of the sutra.
Regarding the fact that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are inconceivable:
This is a general praise of the Triple Gem.
For a bodhisattva, there is no teacher;
that they spontaneously generate the bodhicitta within this sutra is called inconceivable.
The latter phrase can be understood as follows:

Although ordinary beings and bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the first stage of the nature-seed (*gotra*) or the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), they are able to maintain non-retrogressive faith throughout successive births and transform others; this is termed "inconceivable."
Regarding the statement that "there is physical distancing but not verbal [distancing]," how is this text to be understood? Furthermore,
by what means has the Bodhisattva been able to perform such inconceivable transformations as described above?
It is entirely because one does not commit evil through the three types of action that one is able to perform inconceivable transformations.
Regarding the physical distancing [from evil], this means severing killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
"Abstaining from speech" means cutting off false speech, harsh speech, and double-tongued speech.
"Neither of body nor speech" means cutting off the three poisons of the mental ground.
The Bodhisattva does not perceive a single dharma such that "this is the body" or "this is karma.

The sixth minister’s exhortation was as follows: "Although I know that the Tathāgata’s mind is impartial and not restricted to any single person, I have personally examined my own grave offenses and dare not go.
The reason for this is my desire to clarify that the Tathāgata has eternally severed birth and death."
It is said that his nature is harmonious and that all his retinue is likewise pure.
My offenses now are grave; I am not among the assembly of the Tathāgata, but am bound for hell.
By what means could I approach the Buddha?
I now deeply lament within myself that I lack the resolve to depart.
Although my crime of killing my father is grave, I have become the sovereign of an entire kingdom.
If I were to go to the Buddha...

If you were to engage me in conversation and speak with me, it would serve my purpose; however, I fear that if you were to do so, I might not respond to your words, which would cause me even greater shame. Therefore, I say that I have no intention of leaving at all.
Regarding the voice that emerged from the sky:
it was because the seventh father-king had exhorted him,
yet King Lokajita’s ministers exhorted him as well, and he still refused to depart.
For this reason, the Father King exhorted him.
Within this, there are three parts.
The first clarifies that it was not long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Second, he spoke of the terrors of coming from hell;
third, he clarified that the bond between father and son is unbroken,
declaring that the Buddha-dharma was about to perish and the Dharma-boat was on the verge of sinking.
"If you do not turn toward the Buddha today, you will surely suffer in hell.
When the king heard this, he fainted and fell to the ground.
My father, who had opposed me, did not consider it wrong; from the air, he exhorted me.
Feeling his father’s compassionate kindness and repenting for being a person of past evil, he heard that his father wished to depart and that no one could save him from his transgressions.
Thus, his heart of repentance surpassed his resentment; this is what is called "fainting.
Regarding the second point: because the roots of humanity in all people have not yet matured.
Furthermore, hearing that the Buddha was departing caused his compassionate heart to be stirred, which is what is meant by "fainting.
It is for the sake of this king that he shall remain in the world for immeasurable kalpas;
this is because the fourth section contains two distinct meanings.
"First, it does not follow that because one has come from within the well-considered superior vows, the Buddha’s superior mind must necessarily be impartial.
Why then must he specifically eliminate my transgressions?
This argument is incorrect."
"Your Majesty, go quickly now to where the Buddha dwells within the twin śāla trees;
upon reaching him, even after immeasurable kalpas, Your Majesty may not know [the truth], yet he will surely eliminate the crime of parricide.
Although the king’s two ministers thus exhorted him to examine his own grave transgression, he was unwilling to go.
From the sky, the Father King uttered a voice, saying: "The Buddha will surely pass away; after that time, there will be no place for you to extinguish your transgressions.
Because of this, he threw himself to the ground, believing that the Buddha had truly passed away.
Therefore, the Tathāgata remained within the twin śāla trees specifically for the sake of the King.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas,
I have now, within a single day, preached the Dharma for the king,
causing him to give rise to liberation and be released from his transgressions.

Just as it is said that "I have dwelt for immeasurable kalpas," this is not different from the two types of response bodies (nirmāṇakāya and sambhogakāya) dwelling in the world and being taught as eternally abiding;
thus, the present non-laxity is likewise not different from dwelling for immeasurable kalpas.
Regarding the six subsequent sections, the first four constitute the "lack of understanding.
As for the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding,
it is through the residence of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) in the world that beings are enabled to attain understanding.
The latter two instances further explain that the Buddha-nature is an eternal dharma.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata does not enter nirvāṇa for the sake of all sentient beings; there is no actual extinction."
This is why other people are not mentioned.
It was because kings such as Śreṇika, believing that the Buddha had entered final extinction, threw themselves to the ground;
therefore, [the Buddha] manifested that he should appear to be extinguished, yet it was not a real extinction.
When I speak of "those who act," I refer to all ordinary beings bound by every fetter; I speak thus for the sake of removing their attachment to emptiness.
This applies universally to Ajātaśatru and all those who have committed the five heinous crimes.
I said that it was for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings who have committed the heinous crimes.
O King of the World, you have now committed a heinous crime; I am preaching the Dharma for this person.
As for what follows, "to benefit them again later," it means:
It is for the sake of sentient beings who cling to the conditioned that [the Buddha] remains long in the world;
it is not for the sake of those who have realized the unconditioned,
for they understand that the eternally abiding does not depend upon his remaining.
Those who act later do not see the Buddha-nature; I must remain in the world to preach for them so that they may understand the Buddha-nature.
If they were to understand the Buddha-nature, there would be no need for me to remain, which is called "not acting."
If it was later performed for others—namely the two assemblies of Ānanda and Kāśyapa—how can you say that he acted solely for King Ajātaśatru?
Furthermore, King Ajātaśatru was actually the consort of the king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, as for what is later called "Buddha-nature," I have made it so that Buddha-nature may arise.
"Ajita" means "fear"; it is precisely because [without my teaching] Buddha-nature would not arise.
The extensive arising of afflictions refers to the birth of enmity.
From "The secret words of the Tathāgata" onwards, there is a praise of the inconceivability of the Triple Gem.
From "The Great Compassionate Guide" onwards, as for the fifth textual passage, why does it come forth?
It arises from two intentions. This is because,
as stated in the preceding passage, there are no skilled physicians in the world who can heal my body and mind.
"You have not yet departed from your home;
therefore, the Tathāgata has entered the Moon-Love Samādhi and emitted divine light that shines upon the King’s body,
removing the suffering of his punishment."
If the King were to approach the Buddha, his grave transgressions would surely be eliminated;
it is for this reason that these words were composed.
Regarding the two intentions mentioned above, the statement "for the sake of the King, remaining until immeasurable kalpas" refers to this.
There are only words regarding conditioned existence, yet no actual conditioned affairs.
The aforementioned statement that he became a king and dwelt in the world is not necessarily true.

Therefore, the Tathāgata emitted the Moon-Love Samādhi to remove the king’s suffering from punishment and bring him out as a layman; thus, the statement that he became a king and dwelt in the world was indeed true and not false.
The reason for mentioning Great Compassion first is to establish that it surpasses even the profoundest King of Loving-kindness and the King who removes heavy transgressions.
It has been heard that people say when the kalpa comes to an end, the three months appear simultaneously everywhere.
Desiring to cause Jīvaka to provide a detailed explanation of the reason for the light,
he therefore manifested doubt and engaged in a dialogue,
stating that this was not the light of jewels and the like from the end of an eon.
He replied again, "This is not the light of the world.
He asked further, "If this is not the light of the three moons shining together,
what or who is it that can emit such light?"
"O Heavenly King, you should know that this 'God among Gods' has answered your question:
he who emits the light is the Tathāgata."
This light has no root.
That which is boundless in measure clarifies that this light comes from the mind of signless wisdom;
it cannot be sought after by means of the senses or measurement.
Regarding the phrase "neither blue nor yellow," it means that [the person] comes from a place that is neither blue nor yellow. Furthermore,
one who observes mindfulness personally examines the gravity of their own transgressions.
This means that the Buddha does not hold [the notion] in his mind as previously stated;
since the Tathāgata’s compassionate light illuminates the body and removes suffering, it is said, "He also sees the essence of mindfulness. Below this, the answer is given by means of the seven sons.
From the first stage up to the sixth stage,
these constitute the six children who are ordinary beings prior to their entry into the stages;
furthermore, this one child is named the seventh child.
Those who act as the king does are ordinary persons.

As for those who have extensively committed acts of immediate retribution, the Tathāgata’s great compassion gives rise to a supreme mind toward these suffering beings, regarding them with universal gravity.
It is, for example, like moonlight, which is able to [cool] all those below it.
The preceding section provides a detailed explanation of the reasons for Candraprabha’s arrival.
From this point onward, his beneficial qualities will be clarified;
herein, there are six parts.

the latter two metaphors clarify the extinguishing of the unwholesome;
and the final metaphor clarifies the names of the "moon-lover" (candrakānta).

yet, why is it that when dwelling together with wicked people,
he experiences the aforementioned light shining upon his body and abiding in coarse suffering?

Śakra Devānām-indra does not dwell with ghosts.
My transgressions are now so grave;
how can I go to see the Buddha?
"If I had gone to see the Buddha,
my body would have fallen into hell;
because I do not go now, I am able to remain for a short while."
Why is this so? The King himself explains below:
"I observe that the Tathāgata’s intention would rather be near a lion or a fierce fire than ever near evil.
That we are 'evil persons' is stated as a truth within the scriptures of our Buddha's family."
"Therefore, I shall not depart.
Following Jīvaka’s reply to the king,
this concludes the sixth major section, which provides further exhortation to the king.
He explained six matters to come and exhort the King. What are these six?
First, it is like a person who, when thirsty, quickly rises to assemble a pure multitude.
Second, the hungry man seeks food;
third, the terrified person seeks rescue;
fourth, the sick person seeks a skilled physician.
Those suffering from the five heats seek shade and coolness;
those suffering from the six colds seek fire.
Your Majesty’s transgression is now grave.
Seeking the Buddha should also be like this.
Why would one not go? This refers to those who are constantly icchantikas.
Why did you just now cite the words of the King that the great ocean does not harbor corpses, or that Śakra Devānām Indra does not dwell with ghosts? Your Majesty has cited them erroneously.
Today, this Nirvāṇa Sūtra is a teaching that leaves nothing unsaid;
it even preaches the Dharma for icchantikas,
let alone those who are not icchantikas, who surely do not fail to receive the salvation of his compassion.
Citing the icchantika to exhort the world,
the King said, "I have heard that the icchantika does not believe in cause and effect and does not attain the principles of meaning."
How could the Tathāgata speak of enmity, fear, or unreality?
Therefore, he again examined [the matter] and replied:
"If there were a real self, then even the elimination of the self would constitute a transgression."
From Jīvaka’s response downward, there are three sections in the detailed explanation of the conduct of icchantikas.
From the beginning up to the point "because their illness increases," the characteristics of the icchantika are clarified.
From the passage "Having dispatched messengers and summoned physicians" onwards,
up to "the second difficulty of being cured," it clarifies that the Sage perceives the spiritual capacities of sentient beings, whether they are complete or incomplete.
From the passage "At that time, he entered the sick person's house" onwards,
it clarifies that the Buddha preached the Dharma for him.
The phrase "for example, there is a person" refers to an icchantika.
Regarding "one who has fallen into a grave illness":
this refers to one who is on the verge of death due to a grave worldly illness;
it is intended to clarify that such a person is about to incur the grave illness known as *icchantika*.

One who dreams at night experiences suffering in the body; when the mind perceives form, it is called "awake," but before it has fully achieved clarity, it is called "night" from the time of being an icchantika until now.
As for "dwelling in one palace," there are originally four pillars that sustain it, which are thus firm.
With three pillars already gone,
only one pillar remains before it collapses; shortly thereafter,
at the time of internal conjunction, the light of the desire realm is extinguished as the nine grades of wholesome states are severed, with eight grades being completely eliminated.
The sole minute vestige of goodness is that which cannot help but exist within the icchantika; it is called the "single pillar" because its capacity for support is so weak.
Those who consume the clarified butter of false views cause the pores of their faith to close, so that external goodness cannot enter.
"Lying in ashes" refers to one whose body relies upon the principle of cause and effect; thus it is called "lying in ashes.
"Eating" refers to using wrong severance (*mithyā-prahāṇa*) to nourish the spirit; thus it is called "eating.
"Lifting a withered tree" refers to a mind devoid of cause and effect, such that every tree is destined to become an icchantika.
"To sit and lie down with monkeys" clarifies that within one lacks right concentration and one gallops among the various sensory objects.
"To place one's trust in false views" means one comes and sinks into the mire of the five desires.
Those who fall from the palaces slander the Bodhisattva Vehicle; those who fall from the tall trees slander the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle;
and those who fall as horses, oxen, or sheep slander the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
The garments of blue, yellow, red,
and white represent the signs of the icchantika-thieves.
"Delighting in laughter" and so forth refers to perverse contemplations that satisfy the mind.
The mention of crows, vultures,
and so forth is a remote metaphor for the icchantikas whose consumption of the wholesome Dharma has been entirely exhausted.
As for the falling out of teeth and hair:
To slander [the teachings] is to lack the wisdom of skillful means that brings about true benefit.
To be naked and so forth, having severed the two virtues of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), is called "being without clothing.
To rest one's head upon a dog signifies that the mind has sunk into a state where there is neither cause nor effect.
One who lies amidst excrement and filth is one whose body is possessed by the ten fetters (*daśa-ānuśaya*).
Furthermore, to walk or stay with the deceased is to be a companion to those who have already become *icchantikas*.
Holding hands signifies the meaning of non-duality;
it clarifies that one shares the same vision as an icchantika.
As for "a path filled with venomous snakes, yet passing through its midst": it means that while the path is fraught with danger, one proceeds through it.
The various views of annihilationism and eternalism are called the "poisonous gallop.
The ten unwholesome actions universally lead to the three realms of existence as their path.
From the five heinous crimes and the ten unwholesome actions, one passes on to the immeasurable hells.
Embracing a woman with disheveled hair is a metaphor for the arising of the eight inversions that entwine one another.
Wearing tree leaves as clothing—
This refers to covering the body with a garment that eliminates [the notions of] permanence and annihilation.
As for "riding a carriage and traveling due south," this indicates a south-pointing chariot.
This person slanders the existence of cause and effect,
regarding sovereigns, ministers, and parents as mere metaphorical interpretations.
Such a person is one who [sees these things] in a dream.
The preceding section clarifies the characteristics of an icchantika through the metaphor of dreaming;
from here on, it clarifies the metaphor of awakening for one who has already become an icchantika.
"The mind gives rise to grief and affliction" means:

Having severed all nine grades of wholesome roots and thus becoming an icchantika, one should be called "Joyful" (huan-xi), which in its underlying meaning refers to "sorrow and affliction" (chou-nao).
From the phrase "various families" (*zhū jiā*) onwards is the second section.
Regarding "various families": those who encounter the wholesome as their cause are termed "relatives" (*qīn-shǔ*).
Although the causal significance of the past is not lost, one looks up with gratitude toward the name of the Sage; yet,
because the transgressions of the past have causes that are subtle, weak, and deficient in their designation,
they cannot support the arising of present, complete, and wholesome roots— thus, the roots are said to be incomplete.
This slight merit, in its intermediate state, is called "dust upon the head.
This merit that has been severed, manifesting while residing in a subtle state, is called "tattered clothing.
That which is like a ruined carriage—having little capacity for transporting objects and being a subtle point of departure supported by past slight merit—is called "a ruined carriage."
"His spiritual resonance manifests as a holy name; he is called a physician.

"Quickly ascend the carriage" means that because the time for his realization of the Way is urgent, he is told to "quickly ascend the carriage. From the passage "Then he reflected within himself" onwards, [the Buddha] first observes his characteristics before intending to preach the Dharma to him.
That faculty is weak; it is called the sign of the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*), and its root is inauspicious.
In the present life, he will certainly become a *icchantika*, and is difficult to cure.
Regarding the divination of days: although the aforementioned messengers were inauspicious, one observes their faculties on the fourth or sixth day, etc.
If one falls ill when both the suns are present, the disease is difficult to cure;
observe that this person possesses unwholesome roots and lacks wholesome roots.
This is the second observation of nature by the astrologer.
This icchantika is by nature prone to committing evil and dislikes all that is wholesome.
Regarding the timing, the third [period] is when one observes the autumn season up until midnight;
during this time, one will certainly fall ill and the disease will be difficult to cure.
Observing the mind of an icchantika,
they are precisely intent on performing evil and not desiring to perform good.
Regarding whether this is determinate or indeterminate:
Having severed the superior grade, one next severs the middle grade;
from the middle and lower grades, proceeding from the manifest to the subtle, one necessarily severs the roots of goodness and becomes fixed as an icchantika.
From the subtle grade, one may give rise to the superior grade; proceeding from the subtle to the manifest, one necessarily gives rise to the roots of goodness—this is called "indefinite."
If there are those with merit and virtue,
having made offerings to a thousand or ten thousand Buddhas in the past, their merit and virtue can effect a cure.
If there are those without merit and virtue, [it cannot].
If one has failed to hope for merit since making offerings to even one or two Buddhas in the past, what benefit is there in an auspicious omen?

As for "being together with the messenger," it means responding according to the conditions of the journey; furthermore, because one contemplates the future while on the road, it is said that [the messenger] is "yet to come. Thus, "coming" refers to that which has not yet arrived.

One who possesses longevity has, in the past, produced wholesome karma that results in the present; and through present wholesomeness, they will further produce [wholesome karma] that results in the future.
One such as this is called "long-lived" and is curable.
Those of short lifespan lack past causes that would induce present goodness, or their present goodness does not induce future goodness; thus, their continuity of merit is severed.
This is what is called "short lifespan," which is incurable.
The two children are the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
It is also said that good and evil constitute the two children.
The concurrent arising of good and evil is called "guilt" (gu).
The mutual opposition of good and evil is called "strife" (dòuzhèng).
Good is weak; evil is strong.
To sever the roots of goodness so that they do not arise is called "seizing the head and pulling out the hair.
To see a person holding the great nature of the Great Root Mantra—which is a metaphor for the Buddha-jewel—and yet being an icchantika who lacks the Buddha-jewel, is called "self-extinction."
One who cuts down trees slanders the Jewel of the Dharma;
one who drags leather by hand slanders the Jewel of the Sangha;
and one who leaves things abandoned on the road [slanders the same].
For the most part, these are evil buddhas who wish to clarify that those who slander the existence of cause and effect are merely abandoned by the Buddha-dharma.
They are like those who hold an empty vessel— a vessel that is void and contains nothing.
This is intended to clarify that icchantikas extensively commit various evils and are utterly devoid of wholesome dharmas.
As for "walking alone without a companion," it means that they take evil people as companions and lack virtuous people or virtuous companions; thus, they possess no goodness.
If I do not go, I would not be a true teacher.
Although the teachers of the world originally intended that such a person must die, they nevertheless go for the sake of their present parents, wives, and children;
yet even though they go, they cannot necessarily cure him.
The Tathāgata is likewise.
If he did not go [to them], he would not be called a Buddha possessed of great compassion.
Although he cannot save those who are currently practicing as icchantikas, he does not fail to act.
It is for the sake of producing merit in future lives that one must preach the Dharma.
As for "those in the south who are not birds":
the south represents the separation from the desire realm; it clarifies that icchantikas are eternally separated from wholesome dharmas.
Regarding "entering the sick person's house":

according to the third sutra text, it is explained that when one preaches for a moment to generate even a small or medium degree of subtle goodness, such that [the defilements] are driven far away, this is called "entering the house."
Regarding those who repeatedly block and repeatedly heat [the mind]:
at first they hear the Dharma and give rise to faith,
but later they again give rise to various views such as nihilism and eternalism, thereby slandering it.
A constriction and pain in the throat signifies that one has severed the excellent path.
Cracks on the tongue signify slandering the absence of the Middle Way.
A sudden increase in body size to an abnormal degree of redness and swelling signifies...
It gives rise to great anger and great greed.
Question: One who tends to the sick takes the past as the cause; thus, one is called a "tender of the sick.
Medicine that accords with their specific capacity is called "preaching the Dharma."
Regarding the question of whether one should subsequently cultivate goodness or give rise to evil, it is asked: "What is the nature of one's intention?
The answer, beginning with the words "The Great Master," is spoken in accordance with the underlying principle.
It refers to one who fundamentally possesses reverence and faith in the Triple Gem.
Regarding those whose feelings of reverence and faith have now ceased:
originally, before they became icchantikas,
they had generated reverence and faith toward the Triple Gem.
Now, to slander the Triple Gem means that the sentiment of reverence and faith has ceased.
Regarding those whose fundamental nature is corrupt and evil:
"corrupt" (piè) refers to their original practice of punishing evil instead of cultivating goodness.
Now, those who are harmonious and kind give rise to evil within favorable conditions.
Originally rooted in the kindness and filial piety born of one's parents,
they now slander the existence of parents and claim to have no heart of reverence.
As for those who previously smelled it:
during the second cycle, they are taught that they will be born with one grade of inferior wholesome fragrance, yet this is not fixed; they will certainly become icchantikas.
As for those who previously touched their bodies:
The third cycle is called "Giving Rise to the Lower Grade" through the teaching of the Dharma;
the middle and upper grades may be termed "Contacting the Body," as one temporarily gives rise to faith at the time of hearing the Dharma.
Later, returning to slander [the teaching], it is said that the name "incense" signifies that the olfactory faculty is indeterminate.
Alternatively, that which is as hard as stone refers to the arising of the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*);
that which is as cold as ice refers to the arising of great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
At times it is as hot as fire, giving rise to great craving;
at other times it is as fleeting as sand, giving rise to the view of annihilation.
Death is certain beyond doubt; in this present life, one will inevitably become an icchantika.
However, he did not say that this person was destined to die;
rather, by manifesting the teaching of the Three Turnings of the Wheel as a cause, it was made clear that one would certainly be reborn in the future.
Thus, based on my present observation, I have foreseen that he will surely come again.
When a worldly physician knows that a patient will surely die, he says, "He will certainly not come back.

This internally corresponds to the end of the day's affairs; it is like the conclusion of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma. However, as for the principle of the Way, there is no certainty that [the patient] will not come back.
The subsequent statement, "appearing now to preach the Dharma," refers to the name based on his current activity.
"Clearly coming again" means that when there is a further occasion for superior and wholesome conditions to arise, he will come again to preach.
"Extinction" (nirvāṇa) signifies returning to the source; it is called "returning home."
It may also be understood that he was converted and brought back home without being given a formal name.
As for the messenger arriving the following day,
it signifies that there will be further virtuous responses in future lives.
"Affairs not yet concluded" refers to the fact that the distribution of medicinal ingredients has not been completed in other regions.

Above, the metaphors listed are very numerous, while those in the application are extremely few.
"The World-Honored One is likewise" corresponds to the preceding analogy of the skilled physician;
"faculties and dispositions" corresponds to the preceding [analogy of] astrology, though it does not correspond to the timing of the divination.
"And yet he preaches the Dharma for them" refers to the aforementioned three cycles of preaching the Dharma— entering the chamber, the fragrance, and touching the body.
This is not the case for those who do not preach the Dharma for icchantikas or ordinary worldlings.
This means that because the Buddha’s great compassion does not allow the afflictions of ordinary beings to cease, he teaches the Dharma for their sake.
Great King, the Tathāgata constantly provides medicine to all who are ill.
